vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
words: To be stuck in a rut
defs: Very busy and fast, in a way that feels out of control
To meet someone by chance, with no plan at all
A short trip you make to do one small necessary job
To feel fear or heavy dislike about something before it happens
Something you do so automatically that it takes no thought
Someone who always does the same things in the same order
To handle two or more demanding things at the same time
To be trapped in a routine that never changes and never improves

vocab.text: Notice the pair: you RUN an errand, but you ARE a creature of habit. One is a job you do, the other is a person you are.

reading.rtitle: The Town That Used to Have a Train
paras: Until 1998, a train came through Ribeira Velha four times a day, and the whole town was a creature of habit. People used to plan the week around the timetable: the 6:40 to the capital, the 11:15 back, the last one at seven in the evening. Farmers would carry crates of oranges onto the platform before sunrise. The station master would shout the name of every stop, even though everybody already knew them. Running errands in the capital was ordinary: you left after breakfast and you were home for dinner.

Then the line closed. Nobody believed it at first. Families had to swap the train for a bus that took twice as long on a bad road, so most people cut back on their trips and some stopped going altogether. The square, which used to be full on Sunday evenings, emptied out. Mornings that used to be hectic became slow and, for a while, a little sad. The station was turned into a warehouse, and then into nothing at all. "I used to dread walking past it," says Dona Zilda, who has lived on the same street for sixty years.

Two years ago a group of neighbors started restoring it. The roof was replaced first, then the wooden benches were stripped and sanded down by hand. Nowadays about thirty people meet there every Saturday morning: some paint, some cook, and some only talk. The work has become second nature to them. Nobody is restless anymore, and nobody is stuck in a rut. "I bump into half the town on that platform now," Dona Zilda says, "and not one of us is waiting for a train."

items.situation: A friend from Sao Paulo asks what your weekday mornings used to be like. Answer in three sentences, and use used to at least twice.
tips: I used to get up before five.
I would leave the house in the dark.
Nowadays the whole morning takes twenty minutes.

items.situation: Someone asks what you do not miss about the city. Name two old habits and say why you do not miss them.
tips: I do not miss the hectic mornings.
I used to dread the traffic on Mondays.
I was stuck in a rut and I did not even know it.

items.situation: Tell me about one habit that disappeared when you moved, and one that survived it.
tips: I used to run errands every single Saturday.
That one is still second nature.
I have cut back on almost everything else.

items.situation: A neighbor says small towns are boring. Answer using would for your old routine and nowadays for this one.
tips: I would spend two hours a day in a car going nowhere.
Nowadays I bump into people I know at the market.

answerkey.title: Reveal the rule in one page
list: used to + verb covers BOTH past states and past repeated actions. When you are not sure, this is the safe one.
would + verb covers past repeated ACTIONS only. It never works with a state: "I would live there" is wrong.
would needs the past to be established first. Say when it was, then use would: "Back then, I would leave before six."
Negative: did not use to. The -d moves to did, so it is use, never used.
Question: Did you use to ...? Never "Do you used to ...?"
One finished action is past simple, not used to: "I left the city in 2015."
Expressions: a creature of habit, an errand, to be stuck in a rut, hectic, to juggle, to dread, to bump into, to swap, second nature, to cut back on, restless, nowadays.
answerkey.note: This is the whole lesson on one screen. Photograph it and use it during the week.

listenings.text: I have been thinking about this a lot lately. I used to get up at ten past five, every single day, and after the first year I never needed an alarm, because it had become second nature. I would leave the house before six so that I could beat the traffic, and I would eat breakfast standing up at the office. On Saturdays I used to run errands from nine until two: the bank, the market, the pharmacy, the vet. I was juggling all of it and I honestly thought that was normal. The strange part is that I was not unhappy. I was busy, which is not the same thing, and it took me years to learn the difference. Nowadays my whole morning takes about twenty minutes, and I still cannot quite believe it.

People ask me whether I miss the city, and the honest answer is that I miss exactly one thing. I do not miss the hectic mornings. I do not miss the meetings that used to eat my whole afternoon, and I certainly do not miss the fact that I would spend two hours a day in a car going nowhere. I was stuck in a rut and I did not even know it. What I do miss is bumping into people. In the city you would run into somebody you knew every time you left the building: the guy from the bakery, an old colleague, somebody's cousin. Out here I have to make an effort, and I have had to cut back on my excuses. So I go to the market on Saturday mornings, even when I do not need anything, because that is where everybody is.

extra_audio.text: First, Paulo says he found an old photo from the office Christmas party. Then Ana admits that she used to dread that party every single year. Next, Paulo explains that he thought she loved it, because she would stay until the very end. After that, Paulo says he has cut back and does not go to the office on Fridays anymore. Finally, Ana invites him to come and see her town for himself.
